flashcards.back: The field around a charge, drawn as lines running from + to -: a positive charge placed in it is pushed along the lines, and E = F/q. Between charged plates the evenly spaced lines mean a uniform field.

The field around a magnet or current, drawn as lines that loop from N to S outside a bar magnet and never cross: the line direction at a point gives the direction of B there, and closer lines mean a stronger field.
The amount of magnetic field threading a coil, Φ = BA cos θ, measured in webers (Wb): it is greatest when the coil faces the field squarely and zero when the coil is edge-on to it.
The induced voltage around a coil when the flux through it changes, emf = -N ΔΦ/Δt: it exists only while the flux is changing, never from flux merely being present.
The induced emf equals the rate of change of flux linkage, emf = -N ΔΦ/Δt, with the minus sign (Lenz's law) saying the induced effect opposes the change that produces it.

The flux looks large inside the coil, so voltage feels like it should be there. No change in flux, no emf: the magnet sitting still gives zero - only motion makes the meter kick. In the animation the needle kicks as the magnet moves into the coil, holds flat the whole time the magnet sits inside it, and kicks the other way as the magnet is pulled out: the meter is reading change, not amount.

items.prompt: A bar magnet is pushed into a coil and then held perfectly still inside it, with a meter connected across the coil. A student claims an emf keeps flowing the whole time. What does the meter actually show?
The flux through a 200-turn coil falls from 0.030 Wb to 0.010 Wb in 0.50 s. Calculate the induced emf, showing your working with Faraday's law.

items.answer: The emf follows the rate of change of flux, not the flux itself. As the coil turns edge-on the flux passes through zero but is changing fastest there, so the emf peaks; half a turn later the flux changes the other way, so the emf reverses and alternates with the spin.
